captions.text: Recap of chapter 34: a coding agent that reads the issue, changes the code and runs the tests.
The model's code ran in a box with no network, little memory and a time limit.
A fix counted only when tests it never saw passed too.
And locking the tests stopped it faking a win.
Most people build agents with frameworks someone else wrote. Today: the same agent in two of them.
Choose a framework by what it does when things go wrong, not by its score.
In LangGraph, an agent is a graph you draw: a node for the model, a node for the tools.
Call the model, and if it asked for tools, run them and go back. Chapter 12's loop, drawn.
That comment matters: without handle_tool_errors, a tool's error ends the whole run.
In Pydantic AI, an agent is an Agent with a model and tools. Here's how it reaches Ollama.
Two settings we had to find: which name the reply limit is sent under, and a note it adds.
The same agent: 8 lines in whitebox, 28 in LangGraph, 35 here. Most extra lines fix a default.
Same bugs, same models, three frameworks. Predict: which scores best?
On Flash-Lite, all three fixed the same nine bugs and missed the same one.
On 7B, the gaps are smaller than the run-to-run spread. The model does the fixing.
So make things go wrong on purpose. A scripted model plays the same fault in each framework.
A wrong-type argument: both frameworks caught it. whitebox ran the tool with it. Our biggest gap.
An empty reply: LangGraph took it as the answer. A tool's error: both frameworks crashed by default.
A cut-off reply fooled all three. No framework handled every fault.
Some problems only show up between the framework and the model. So we saved what it sent.
Pydantic AI added a second system message we never wrote, about <system> tags.
14B then wrote fake <system> messages, invented a bug report, and never read the real one.
14B on the hard bugs. Every gap has a cause.
LangGraph crashed four times when Ollama aborted a reply. It doesn't retry unless you add a RetryPolicy.
Pydantic AI went from 0 to 4 when we left its note out.
Last, switching models. Gemini 3.6 Flash thinks, and its thinking counts against the reply limit.
At chapter 34's 1,024 tokens: 6 of 10. At 8,192: all 10. One number.
Make it fail on purpose, one fault at a time, and write down what it does.
Save what it sends, and compare it with what you wrote.
Read its defaults: retries, limits, and what happens to a tool's error.
LangGraph installed 49 packages, Pydantic AI 36. Pin the version you tested.
And run your own eval, on your own model, before and after any change.
Five exercises: a type check, a retry, a scripted model, spotting added messages, and a score table.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

captions.text: A framework saves you writing a loop. It doesn't save you understanding one.
You've built one, so you can read theirs.
